content: Gray hair typically develops naturally as individuals age, transitioning from their original hair color to gray and eventually to white. By the age of 40, over 40% of Americans exhibit some degree of gray hair, although white hairs can emerge as early as childhood. The onset of graying is predominantly determined by genetic factors. In certain cases, individuals may be born with gray hair due to inherited genetic traits. Many people opt to use hair dye to conceal the presence of gray hair. The change in hair color is attributed to a gradual reduction in pigmentation, which occurs when melanin production ceases in the hair root. As a result, new hair grows without pigment. Two specific genes, Bcl2 and Mitf, are believed to play a significant role in the graying process. At the base of hair follicles, stem cells are responsible for generating melanocytes, which are the cells that produce and store pigment in both hair and skin. The death of these melanocyte stem cells is the primary cause of graying. In some instances, gray hair may also result from a vitamin B12 deficiency or an imbalance in thyroid function.
